hook: A republic born out of defeat, and painters the Salon keeps rejecting.

art.credit: Gustave Caillebotte, Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877

world.governs: The Third Republic is new and fragile. Monarchists hold a majority in parliament until 1877.
world.everyday: Most French people still live in the countryside. Paris is being rebuilt along Haussmann's wide boulevards.
world.arts: The Impressionists show outside the official Salon, and Zola is writing his Rougon-Macquart novels.
world.meanwhile: Germany has just united under Prussia, and Japan is racing to modernise.

cards.title: A republic born out of defeat
cards.text: France lost its war with Prussia in 1871. The new Third Republic is fragile, and most French people still live and work in the countryside.

cards.title: Painting outside the Salon
cards.text: Painters the official Salon keeps rejecting decide to show their work on their own, in a photographer's former studio on the Boulevard des Capucines.
A doctor turned politician. Mayor of Montmartre during the siege of 1870, now a fierce critic of the government from the left.
One of the few women at the centre of the new painting. She shows her work at the first independent exhibition.
A critic mocks Monet's Impression, Sunrise, and gives the movement its name.

doors.text: Japan opens up to the world
Twenty years on: the Dreyfus affair

hook: Electric light, cabarets, and a trial that tears France in two.

art.credit: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, At the Moulin Rouge, 1892–95

world.governs: The Republic lives through scandal after scandal: Panama in 1892, then the Dreyfus affair.
world.everyday: Electric light, the bicycle craze and, from 1898, the digging of the first metro line change city life.
world.arts: Montmartre cabarets, Toulouse-Lautrec's posters, and in 1895 the Lumière brothers' first film screenings.
world.meanwhile: Britain is at the height of Queen Victoria's empire, and Japan has just defeated China in 1895.

cards.title: Electric light and a divided country
cards.text: The Eiffel Tower, built for the 1889 World's Fair, stands over a city of cafés and cabarets. Beneath the glitter, one trial is tearing France in two.

cards.kicker: Setting the scene · the Dreyfus affair
cards.title: A captain convicted on forged evidence
cards.text: In 1894 Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish army officer, is convicted of treason and sent to Devil's Island. The evidence against him does not hold up.
The most famous novelist in France. Taking Dreyfus's side will cost him a conviction for libel and almost a year of exile in England.
Out of parliament since the Panama scandal cost him his seat, he writes for the newspaper L'Aurore.
A Polish student who came to Paris in 1891. Working in a shed with Pierre Curie, she is about to change physics.

doors.text: Japan opens up to the world

hook: The shogun is gone, the samurai lose their swords, and the first trains run.

art.credit: Kobayashi Kiyochika, Shin-Ōhashi Bridge in the Rain, Tokyo, 1876

world.governs: Former samurai rule in the emperor's name. The old feudal domains are abolished in 1871.
world.everyday: Most people still farm. From 1873 the land tax is paid in money instead of rice.
world.arts: Woodblock prints show trains, gas lamps and brick streets, and Western painting is taught for the first time.
world.meanwhile: France has just lost a war and become a republic again, and the United States marks its centennial in 1876.

cards.title: Edo becomes Tokyo
cards.text: In 1868 the shogunate fell. The teenage emperor moved into Edo Castle, and the city was renamed Tokyo, the eastern capital.

cards.kicker: Setting the scene · a country in a hurry
cards.title: Catching up with the West
cards.text: Railways, telegraphs, a new army and new schools arrive within a few years. In 1876 the samurai lose their stipends and the right to carry swords.
Emperor since he was fourteen, he becomes the face of the new Japan, photographed in Western uniform.
A farmer's son adopted into a samurai family, he sailed to London as a young man to study. He will later write Japan's first constitution.

art.credit: Utagawa Hiroshige III, steam train at Yokohama, 1874

doors.text: A republic born out of defeat
How the Tokugawa came to power

hook: A foot soldier's son rules Japan, and his tea master pays the price.

world.governs: Hideyoshi rules through the great lords. Peasants were disarmed in the sword hunt of 1588.
world.everyday: Farmers are tied to their fields by the land survey, and Kyoto is enclosed by new earthen walls.
world.arts: Gold-leaf screens by the Kanō painters, and the quiet, plain tea of Rikyū.
world.meanwhile: In England, Elizabeth I has just beaten the Armada. In 1592 Hideyoshi sends his armies into Korea.

cards.title: After a century of civil war
cards.text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi has brought the warring lords to heel. For the first time in generations, Japan answers to one ruler.
Born the son of a foot soldier, now the most powerful man in Japan. He builds lavishly and loves the tea ceremony.
Hideyoshi's tea master. He turns tea into an art of plain, quiet beauty: wabi.

cards.title: Counted field by field
cards.text: Most people farm. Hideyoshi's great land survey measures every field and fixes who owes how much rice in tax.
Hideyoshi's strongest ally, sent east to rule from a small castle town called Edo. He is waiting.

doors.text: Three centuries on, Edo becomes Tokyo
A republic born out of defeat

hook: The king moves his court to Versailles.

world.governs: Louis XIV rules alone, and in 1682 moves the court and government to Versailles.
world.everyday: Most people are peasants paying taxes, tithes and dues. In 1685 the Protestant faith is banned.
world.arts: Lully's operas and Le Nôtre's gardens set the taste of Europe.
world.meanwhile: Edo-period Japan is at peace, and Bashō is writing his haiku.

hook: A teenage girl lifts a siege.

world.governs: France is split by the Hundred Years' War. The English and their Burgundian allies hold the north.
world.everyday: Villages have been raided for decades, and the Black Death keeps returning.
world.arts: Books are still copied by hand. Christine de Pizan writes from a convent.
world.meanwhile: In China, the Ming treasure fleets are about to make their last voyage.

hook: Court women write The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book.

world.governs: The emperor reigns, but the Fujiwara family rules as regents.
world.everyday: Most people farm rice far from the capital and pay their taxes in kind.
world.arts: Court women write in kana: The Tale of Genji, The Pillow Book.
world.meanwhile: In China, the Song dynasty is in its first decades. In France, the Capetian kings are new.

hook: Hokusai's Great Wave, in a city of a million.

art.credit: Katsushika Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa, c. 1831

world.governs: The Tokugawa shoguns still rule a country closed to most foreigners.
world.everyday: Edo is one of the largest cities in the world, and the Tenpō famine strikes in the 1830s.
world.arts: Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji and Hiroshige's Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō.
world.meanwhile: In Britain the first passenger railways run, and France has a new king after the revolution of 1830.

hook: Shakespeare's theatre and an ageing queen.

art.credit: Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I, c. 1588

world.governs: Elizabeth I is old and has no heir. Protestant England is at war with Spain.
world.everyday: London is growing fast, crowded, and often hit by plague.
world.arts: Shakespeare's company opens the Globe on Bankside in 1599.
world.meanwhile: In Japan, Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara in 1600.

hook: The Tang capital, its poets and the Silk Road.

art.credit: Liang Kai, Li Bai Strolling, 13th century

world.governs: The Tang dynasty is at its height under Emperor Xuanzong, until the An Lushan rebellion of 755.
world.everyday: Chang'an is one of the largest cities in the world, its markets full of goods from the Silk Road.
world.arts: Li Bai and Du Fu write the poems that define Chinese poetry.
world.meanwhile: In Japan, the Great Buddha of Nara is dedicated in 752.
